action.question: Which monitoring mechanism should the manager use?

questions.question: Which monitoring mechanism should the manager use?

options.label: A. Per-manager /loop (20 min)
options.description: Manager arms /loop 20m /manage tick when it has workers; disarms when none. Lightweight, uses existing primitives, ~3 cache-miss model invocations/hour. Recommended starting point.

options.label: B. Centralized watchdog daemon
options.description: Write a launchd-managed manager-watchdog.py that scans all manager state files every 5 min, only nudges managers with actual problems (stale/dead workers). Heavier to build, but matches your 'signal to all managers' framing and is more resilient.

options.label: C. Both A + B
options.description: Per-manager loop normally; centralized watchdog as a safety net. Most resilient, most code.

options.label: D. Event-driven only (no periodic)
options.description: On dispatch, manager schedules ONE check at an expected-by deadline (e.g. 30 min after spawn). No periodic. Cheapest but misses slow hangs.

questions.question: If A or C is picked, what tick interval?

options.label: 20 minutes (recommended)
options.description: Past the 5-min prompt-cache TTL anyway; amortizes the cache miss against a longer wait. ~3 ticks/hour.

options.label: 5 minutes (your example)
options.description: Pays the cache miss every tick. ~12 ticks/hour. Faster anomaly detection but noticeably more model invocations.

options.label: Skip — B-only or D-only
options.description: Don't need an interval (centralized watchdog handles cadence, or event-driven has no period).

transcript_tail.text: Good catch — the worker has no instruction in `/close-work` to report back to the manager once it's done. Without that, my state log stays "in progress" forever even though the work merged. Let me look at the current close-work flow and add the manager-report step.
Adding the manager-report step to both the Phase 5 close path and the Handoff brief section.
The close-work skill now reports completion (or handoff) back to the spawning manager. Let me update the `/manage` skill to cross-reference this so the loop is fully documented from both sides.

Done. Two surgical edits, no impact on Worker A in flight.

## What I changed

**`close-work` SKILL.md** — added Phase 5 step 9 (and a parallel paragraph in the Handoff brief section):

- Worker detects whether it was spawned by a manager (`REMOTE_CONTROL_REPLY_TO` env var or `[from cse_*]` header on the first turn).
- If yes, after the merge/push/lease-release/ticket-close are all done, the worker submits a final user-turn back into the manager via send-to-session with the merge SHA, leases released, verification one-liner, and any caveats.
- If neither signal is present, the step is skipped — human-driven sessions get no behavior change.

**`manage` SKILL.md — Play: close** — updated to reflect that the close-work skill now self-reports:

- The boss-OK message no longer needs to ask the worker to "reply when done" explicitly — close-work's step 9 covers it.
- Added routing for the **handoff** case too (worker reports `/close-work handoff:` → manager marks state `handoff`, leaves row active for resume-work).

## Why this matters for the loop

Without step 9, the manager's state log would stay "in progress" forever even after the worker merged and the one-shot server self-exited — no signal would arrive. Step 9 closes the loop on both sides:

- **Pre-close**: worker reports status → boss OKs (custom brief instruction, already in Worker A's brief)
- **Post-close**: worker reports completion after merge/cleanup land (new close-work step 9, applies to all future workers)

## Effect on Worker A

Worker A's brief already says "WAIT for my OK before /close-work" — the pre-close handshake stands. When I eventually OK and tell it to /close-work, it will hit the new step 9 inside close-work and self-report the completion. No re-prompt needed.

The manager should be triggered to monitor its, uh, sessions. It says triggered sessions. Um, maybe we can have a, uh, timed, um, five minute pack, um, five minute signal given to all managers somehow, or if you have any other suggestions on how the manager could periodically track by the time it launches off of monitor or or, um, at some point in time to make sure that the sessions are not stale.

Good idea. Right now the manager only wakes when the boss types or a worker replies — silent worker deaths go unnoticed. Let me weigh the options before changing anything.

## How the manager could self-monitor

| Option | How it works | Cost | Failure modes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Per-manager `/loop`** | At first dispatch, manager runs `/loop 20m /manage tick`. Each tick runs the **status** play silently — only surfaces anomalies (worker self-exited without reporting, disconnected >30 min, hung, `requires_action` permission prompt waiting). Stops when no active workers. | ~3 model invocations/hour while workers exist; mostly silent | Manager session crashes → loop chain breaks; new manager session has to re-arm |
| **B. Centralized watchdog (launchd)** | A new daemon (`~/dev/ai-harness/manager-watchdog.py`) scans `~/.ai-harness/manager/*.jsonl` every 5 min, finds active workers, joins with `sessions --json`, sends a `[from watchdog]` alert into the manager **only when something's wrong** + the manager is idle. | Daemon + plist to maintain; near-zero token cost (only nudges on anomalies) | Daemon goes down → silent gap; sister process to the existing usage-limit monitor, similar lifecycle |
| **C. Hybrid (A + B)** | Per-manager loop is the normal cadence; watchdog is a safety net for crashed managers. | A's cost + B's daemon | Most resilient; most code to write |
| **D. Event-driven only** | On each dispatch, manager calls `/loop` once with a deadline (e.g. "check at 30 min after spawn"). One scheduled check per worker, not periodic. | Lightest model cost | Doesn't catch slow-drift hangs |

**Cache math note**: 5-minute interval falls on the prompt-cache TTL boundary — every tick pays a cache miss. 20-minute interval is past the TTL anyway, so amortizes the miss against a longer interval. So if A or C, I'd recommend 20 min not 5 min.

**On "signal given to all managers"** — that's literally what B does. It's the cleanest match for your phrasing, and it's a near-twin of the existing usage-limit monitor architecturally (scan-all-sessions daemon → act on anomalies → send a turn).

## My recommendation

**Start with A** (per-manager `/loop` at 20 min). It's the smallest change — just an edit to the `/manage` skill telling the manager to arm `/loop` after a dispatch and disarm when no active workers. Catches 95% of cases. We can add B as a separate ticket if A's "manager crashed → loop dies" gap actually bites.

But if you'd rather build the centralized one once and not worry about it, B is the cleaner end-state.
